name: Annual magistrate lists (consuls, tribunes, dictators, extraordinary offices)
producing_institution: Roman pontifical/annalistic record-keeping; the libri lintei (linen books) kept in the temple of Juno Moneta
institution_evidence: Livy IV.13 explicitly cites the libri lintei as the documentary basis for the annona prefecture ('in libros linteos utroque anno relatum inter magistratus praefecti nomen'); the eponymous-magistrate list is the one early-republican dataset whose existence is directly attested inside the pilot passages.
period: Roman Republic, 5th c. BCE onward (compiled later)
survival_status: Survives mediated: fasti Capitolini (fragmentary, Augustan), Livy's and Dionysius's lists; the libri lintei themselves lost
notes: The backbone join-key for every other reconstructed table: Roman events are dated by consular year.

name: Census of private grain stocks with household quotas (Minucian declarations)
producing_institution: praefectura annonae (L. Minucius, 440 BCE), an extraordinary magistracy
institution_evidence: Livy IV.12 describes the procedure in operational terms: 'profiteri cogendo frumentum et vendere, quod usui menstruo superesset, fraudandoque parte diurni cibi servitia' — compulsory declaration, a monthly-use threshold, forced sale of surplus, ration cuts. A declaration process implies records of declarations; no values survive and the fifth-century institutional capacity for such a census is doubted by modern scholarship (the episode may retroject late-republican annona practice).
survival_status: No documents survive; procedure known only through Livy's narrative
notes: KEY instance of a described-but-lost administrative dataset. The structure (declarant, stock, threshold, forced sale) is Livy's own; only its historicity, not its narrative existence, is in question.

name: Public grain sale-price decisions over time
producing_institution: Senate (price deliberation: 'agitatum in senatu, quanti plebi daretur'); quaestors/aediles for execution
institution_evidence: Two attested data points in the pilot corpus: the 491 BCE Senate price debate (Livy II.34, decision process attested, value not) and the 439 BCE distribution of Maelian grain 'assibus in modios aestimatum' = 1 as per modius (Livy IV.16). A SERIES is a reconstruction; the early Republic had no standing annona administration, so continuous price records are unlikely to have existed — flagging the series itself as a structure the narrative implies only episodically.
period: Rome, 5th c. BCE episodes; systematic only from C. Gracchus's lex frumentaria (123 BCE)
notes: Tests Livy's counterfactual (price concessions convertible to constitutional concessions) and Machiavelli's withholding reframing: with price data one could distinguish 'expensive grain' from 'no grain' regimes.

name: Emergency grain procurement missions: routes, agents, outcomes
producing_institution: Consuls (492 BCE: 'dimissis passim ad frumentum coemendum'); praefectus annonae and legationes (440 BCE: 'multis circa finitimos populos legationibus terra marique... missis')
institution_evidence: Livy II.34 preserves a route-by-outcome breakdown (Etruria: delivered via Tiber; Cumae: purchased, ships seized; Volsci/Pomptine: purchase refused, agents endangered; Sicily: delivered next year) — the narrative shape of a procurement log. Whether the consuls kept written accounts in 492 BCE is undemonstrable; public purchasing implies at minimum accounting to the aerarium, attested institutionally only later.
notes: Machiavelli compresses this entire table to 'mandato per grani in Sicilia' (one row, two columns). The procurement log is precisely what his chancery self produced in Florentine provisioning correspondence — see reports/initial_report.md §6 on the Florentine analogue (the Abbondanza magistracy's records).

name: Recipient registers of grain distributions (public sales and private largesses)
producing_institution: None attested for the 5th c. BCE; recipient lists (recensus of the plebs frumentaria) are attested only for the late-republican/imperial annona
institution_evidence: No evidence any register of Maelius's beneficiaries or of 5th-century public distributions existed. Livy's 'plebem hoc munere delinitam... secum trahere' asserts the recipient→follower link narratively without documentary basis. Classified C: a modern researcher would need it to test the largesse→partisan mechanism; its ancient existence cannot be established.
period: hypothetical for 440 BCE; real analogues from 123 BCE (Gracchan frumentationes) and the imperial plebs frumentaria
survival_status: Nonexistent for the period; later analogues epigraphically attested
notes: The cleanest case of a Machiavellian proposition (private food → partisans → tyranny risk) whose test requires a dataset that the narrated period could not have produced — but which Renaissance Florence DID produce (the Abbondanza's distribution records, Medici benefaction ricordi), suggesting the mechanism's data-model is Florentine in texture.

name: Register of ager publicus occupation: possessor, area, tenure status
producing_institution: None for the early Republic; censors recorded citizen property (census) from the mid-Republic; Gracchan land commission (IIIviri a.d.a.) demonstrably surveyed and marked boundaries (surviving termini Gracchani)
institution_evidence: Livy II.41 presupposes identifiable 'possessores' of public land ('quem publicum possideri a privatis criminabatur') and the Licinian-Sextian cap presupposes measurable holdings — but no early-republican cadastre is attested; enforcement anecdotes (Licinius Stolo's own violation) suggest self-declaration, not survey. The Gracchan commission's boundary stones (3 survive with commissioners' names) are the first hard evidence of systematic land registration — exactly when Machiavelli's narrative reactivates the law.
period: structure implied 486-367 BCE; first attested instruments 133-121 BCE
survival_status: Termini Gracchani (CIL I²) survive; no registers
notes: Machiavelli's 'non si potesse possedere per alcuno cittadino più che tanti iugeri' presupposes this register's existence to be enforceable — his implicit data model exceeds the period's attested administrative capacity. Note his vagueness: 'più che TANTI iugeri' (so-many iugera) — he does not know or does not repeat the 500-iugera figure.

name: Colony enrollment rolls: volunteers by name, origin, allotment
producing_institution: Colonial commissions (triumviri coloniae deducendae / agro dando), named at Livy III.1: T. Quinctius, A. Verginius, P. Furius
institution_evidence: Livy III.1 describes the procedure generating the record: 'iussi nomina dare, qui agrum accipere vellent' — enrollment BY NAME before a named three-man commission, with a quota ('ad explendum numerum') that could be monitored (hence the known shortfall and Volscian back-fill). A name-list with a quota is a register by definition; none survives.
period: Rome, 5th c. BCE onward; procedure continuously attested into the late Republic
survival_status: No early rolls survive; late-republican/imperial colonial land registers (formae) attested
notes: The one pilot dataset where BOTH authors engage the record: Livy reports the enrollment shortfall as data ('adeoque pauci nomina dedere'), and Machiavelli explicitly flags it as a 'termine notabile'. His distance-decay hypothesis is testable in principle against enrollment rates × colony distance — a genuinely operationalizable Machiavellian claim.

name: Political trial log: accusations of powerful citizens, forum, judges, outcome, attendant violence
producing_institution: Tribunician prosecution before the popular assembly (diem dicere, Livy II.35); quaestorian perduellio prosecution (Livy II.41, one tradition); records if any in the aerarium/annalistic tradition
institution_evidence: Both pilot trials are narratively rich: Coriolanus (tribunes set the day, condemned in absentia) and Cassius (two variant procedures preserved — paternal judgment vs quaestors, with Livy preferring the public trial 'idque propius fidem est'). Livy's variant-handling shows the record was already unstable in antiquity. Florentine counterpart fully attested: the Otto di Guardia's deliberazioni Machiavelli invokes ('otto giudici') generated surviving registers.
period: Rome, 5th c. BCE (as narrated); Florence 1494-1512 (attested archives)
survival_status: Roman: narrative only. Florentine: archival series survive (ASF, Otto di Guardia)
notes: This is THE dataset for Machiavelli's central I.7 claim. Strikingly, the Florentine half of his own comparison is documentable from archives he knew professionally — his cross-polity design (Rome/Clusium/Valori/Soderini) is data-feasible on the Florentine side only.

name: Patron-client and benefaction network: who owes whom what, mobilization capacity
producing_institution: None (Rome: clientela was customary, not registered); Florence: partially self-documenting through family ricordanze, dowry contracts (Monte delle doti), and debt instruments
institution_evidence: Livy attests the network's OPERATION, not its registration: clients deployed to break up meetings (II.35), Maelius's procurement 'per hospitum clientiumque ministeria' (IV.13), the shared workforce as intelligence channel (IV.13). Machiavelli's benefit typology — lending money, dowering daughters, protecting from magistrates (III.28) — matches documented Florentine instruments (loans, Monte delle doti, favor with the Otto), each of which DID generate records in Florence.
period: customary at Rome; documentable in Florence 15th-16th c.
survival_status: Roman: none. Florentine: rich archival analogues (ricordanze, notarial acts)
notes: Strongest pilot evidence for the working hypothesis's category 2 (professional/administrative experience shaping the data model): Machiavelli's private-reputation variable decomposes into exactly the benefit types that Florentine records tracked.

name: Popular unrest event series: secessions, tumults, near-lynchings, suicides, with triggers and resolution channel
producing_institution: No Roman institution logged unrest as such; the annalistic tradition (via pontifical tabulae?) preserved event skeletons. Florence: the Signoria's and the Otto's registers did effectively log tumults
institution_evidence: Constructed from narrative: the pilot passages alone yield a near-lynching channeled to trial (II.35), mass suicides under rationing (IV.12, 'multi ex plebe... se in Tiberim praecipitaverunt'), a lynching-equivalent by state agent (IV.14). The trigger-domain and resolution-channel codings are OUR analytic variables, derived from Machiavelli's roba/onori and ordinario/straordinario distinctions — flagged to avoid circularity: using them to test his claims on LIVY's events is legitimate; using Machiavelli-selected events alone is not.
period: Rome 5th c. BCE (narrated); scalable to all of Livy I-X
notes: The full-corpus version of this table (every unrest event in Livy I-X, Machiavelli-cited or not) is the key instrument against Machiavelli's selection bias — it supplies the denominator his case-picking hides.

name: Mobilization capacity assessments: manpower, morale, grievance freshness
producing_institution: None attested for the Volsci; Rome's census served this function for Rome itself; Renaissance states produced exactly such assessments (Machiavelli's own legation dispatches and Ordinanza memoranda)
institution_evidence: Livy II.35 stages Coriolanus and Attius Tullius REASONING over mobilization variables (youth lost to wars and pestilence, broken spirits, stale hatred needing fresh provocation) — strategic-intelligence analysis without a document. Machiavelli omits this entire layer from I.7, yet it is the closest Livian analogue to his own professional genre (the chancery situation report).
period: narrated 491 BCE; Florentine analogues 1499-1512 (attested, published in his legazioni)
survival_status: Roman side: none. Machiavelli's own dispatches survive
notes: Included to document a PILOT NEGATIVE RESULT against over-claiming: where Livy offers the most chancery-like material in Case A, Machiavelli does not engage it. Administrative experience does not make him preserve administrative detail; his compression is driven by the proposition under argument, not by professional affinity.

name: Punitive confiscation and liquidation: goods seized, sale proceeds, memorial sanctions
producing_institution: Quaestors (Livy IV.15: 'iubere itaque quaestores vendere ea bona atque in publicum redigere' — ordered to sell and pay into the treasury); aerarium accounting
institution_evidence: Strongest attested fiscal-administrative procedure in the pilot: both condemnations end in documented-type acts — Maelius's goods sold by quaestors into the public treasury, house razed with a toponym preserved (Aequimelium); Cassius's property consecrated to Ceres with an INSCRIBED statue ('ex Cassia familia datum') that Livy treats as evidence. Livy is here reading material records (toponym, inscription) — and telling us so.
period: Rome, 485 and 439 BCE (as narrated); quaestorian aerarium practice continuously attested later
survival_status: Inscription and toponym reported by Livy; no account books
notes: Machiavelli omits all of it. The confiscation apparatus — the state's fiscal unwinding of dangerous private wealth — is administratively the mirror-image of his 'keep the public rich, citizens poor' maxim, yet he never cites the mechanism that enforced it.
